name: COLQ-related congenital myasthenic syndrome (endplate acetylcholinesterase deficiency)

clinicalPearls: COLQ encodes the collagenic tail (ColQ) that anchors acetylcholinesterase within the synaptic basal lamina; loss of function produces a synaptic (endplate) acetylcholinesterase deficiency rather than a receptor or presynaptic defect.

Presents typically in the neonatal period or infancy with axial and limb-girdle weakness, hypotonia, ptosis, ophthalmoparesis, delayed motor milestones and fatigable weakness that worsens through the day.
A characteristic slow, sluggishly reactive pupil (delayed pupillary light response) is a well-recognised clue and helps distinguish this subtype from most other congenital myasthenic syndromes.

Repetitive compound muscle action potential on a single supramaximal nerve stimulus (a repetitive CMAP) reflects prolonged acetylcholine action from absent esterase and is a hallmark electrophysiological finding.

Crucially, acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine and related agents) are ineffective and typically harmful or even dangerous, as further prolonging acetylcholine dwell time worsens endplate injury.
Sympathomimetic and ephedrine-type agents, and salbutamol/albuterol, are the mainstay of pharmacological benefit in this subtype.
Spinal deformity, notably scoliosis with a rigid spine, and respiratory insufficiency may evolve over time and warrant proactive surveillance.
reference.pathophysiology: COLQ-related congenital myasthenic syndrome is a synaptic (endplate) disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in COLQ, the gene encoding the collagen-like tail subunit that tethers the catalytic subunits of acetylcholinesterase to the synaptic basal lamina of the neuromuscular junction. ColQ both anchors the enzyme in the synaptic cleft, via interaction with perlecan/dystroglycan and MuSK, and clusters it opposite the postsynaptic folds. When ColQ is absent or non-functional, acetylcholinesterase cannot be positioned in the cleft, so released acetylcholine is not hydrolysed and lingers, repeatedly reactivating acetylcholine receptors. This causes cationic (particularly calcium) overload of the postsynaptic region, desensitisation and depolarisation block of receptors, and a slow degenerative endplate myopathy with loss of junctional folds and nerve-terminal encroachment. The net effect is impaired safety margin of neuromuscular transmission producing fatigable weakness, compounded by structural endplate damage; because the primary problem is failure to clear acetylcholine, anticholinesterase drugs aggravate rather than relieve the defect.
additionalDifferentials: Other congenital myasthenic syndromes, particularly the slow-channel syndrome, which shares a repetitive CMAP and worsens with anticholinesterases
DOK7 and other postsynaptic limb-girdle congenital myasthenic syndromes
Autoimmune myasthenia gravis (seronegative in young children) and neonatal transient myasthenia
Spinal muscular atrophy and other early-onset motor neuron or anterior horn disorders
Congenital myopathies and congenital muscular dystrophies presenting with hypotonia and ptosis
Infantile botulism and other presynaptic transmission disorders
additionalInvestigations: Repetitive nerve stimulation showing a decremental response and, characteristically, a repetitive CMAP after a single stimulus
Single-fibre electromyography demonstrating increased jitter and blocking
Targeted COLQ sequencing within a congenital myasthenic syndrome gene panel and confirmatory biallelic variant analysis
Slit-lamp or bedside assessment of the pupillary light response to document the slow pupil
Serum acetylcholine receptor and MuSK antibodies to exclude autoimmune myasthenia
Spine imaging and formal respiratory function testing including overnight oximetry where indicated
redFlags: Clinical deterioration or cholinergic crisis after a trial of anticholinesterase medication
Progressive respiratory insufficiency, nocturnal hypoventilation or recurrent aspiration
Rapidly progressive scoliosis or rigid-spine deformity compromising ventilation
Bulbar weakness with feeding difficulty and failure to thrive in infancy
reference.prognosis: Long-term outlook is variable and depends on disease severity and respiratory involvement; many patients stabilise or improve with sympathomimetic therapy, but some experience progressive weakness, spinal deformity and respiratory compromise requiring ventilatory support. Avoidance of anticholinesterase drugs is essential to prevent iatrogenic deterioration.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the disorder as autoimmune myasthenia and prescribing an anticholinesterase, which characteristically worsens COLQ-CMS.
Interpreting a repetitive CMAP as artefact rather than recognising it as a diagnostic clue shared only with the slow-channel syndrome.
Overlooking the slow pupillary light response, a useful and easily missed bedside sign.
Failing to distinguish this synaptic subtype from postsynaptic subtypes such as DOK7 that also respond to salbutamol but tolerate different adjuncts.

management: Sympathomimetic therapy with salbutamol or ephedrine as the pharmacological mainstay
Strictly avoid acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as pyridostigmine, which are ineffective and worsen endplate injury
Respiratory surveillance with overnight oximetry and lung-function testing, and non-invasive ventilation for hypoventilation or crises
Physiotherapy and orthopaedic management of scoliosis and contractures
Confirm the diagnosis by biallelic COLQ analysis and provide genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder
Coordinated care through a specialist neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
